title: Thorn, the lost letter of "Ye Olde"
hook: The "ye" in "Ye Olde" was never meant to be read with a y sound.
peek: "Ye Olde Tea Shoppe" was never pronounced with a y. The "ye" is "the", written with thorn, an old English letter for the th sound. Early printers lacked it and swapped in a y, which looked similar.
lede: Old English had a letter for the th sound: þ, called thorn. In handwriting it gradually came to look a lot like a y. When printing reached England in the fifteenth century, type cast for other European languages had no thorn, so printers used y in its place. "Ye" in old texts is simply "the", and it was said that way.

bullets.text: Fake-archaic shop names such as "Ye Olde Tea Shoppe" became popular centuries later, as a playful nod to the past. Most people now say "yee", but a fifteenth-century reader seeing that word would have said "the".
There was also a genuine separate word "ye", meaning you, as in "hear ye". It comes from a different root and was said with a y, which helped the confusion stick.
Thorn has not vanished everywhere. Icelandic still uses it in everyday writing, along with its cousin eth, ð, which English also once used for the same th sounds.
Early printers helped fix English spelling at the same time that the sound of its long vowels was changing. Many oddities of written English date from that period.
English also dropped wynn, ƿ, for the w sound, which scribes gradually replaced with w, and yogh, ȝ, used for sounds like the old one in "night".
The thorn story is a reminder that the tools of type, from medieval metal sorts to modern fonts like Helvetica, quietly shape how words look.
